Essay:
We plan to adopt the Swedish Return System.
Similar to Swedish Return System, FairPrice can sell reusable shopping baskets made out of	recyclable materials. When customers return this shopping basket, it will refund them for the basket and thus incentivizing them to recycle and reduce littering. Furthermore, at the end of the lifespan, customers can exchange their old basket with a new one and the old one will be recycled.


Benefits

The use of the swedish return system creates a circular economy. The baskets are also lightweight and durable (lasting approximately 15 years). Therefore reducing the number of waste being sent to the landfill. When it does come to the end of its lifespan, the basket can be recycled, leading to 

it will create a sustainable and environmentally friendly way for consumers.



This can also bring about benefits to other businesses, especially smes, after singaporeans gained the habit of bringing their own basket for grocery shopping. The baskets are also easier to clean than plastic or cloth bags.


Challenges and Mitigation

Integrity - There is a risk that customers may not return the crates. Thus, potentially resulting in a constant shortage of available crates as well as an economic disadvantage for the production of more crates to compensate for the lost ones. This could be mitigated by implementing a tracking system on the rental and return activities using membership cards or accounts upon collection of the crates. A penalty can be incurred on the membership accounts for those who do not return by a specific time frame. 


Cost to sustain programme -  Initiating and sustaining a basket deposit scheme would require capital spending in infrastructure, such as deposit points and processing facilities. FairPrice would have to allocate resources for transportation and sorting of returned containers, increasing the cost of logistical operations

 Consumer Convenience -  it can cause inconvenience to customers that have to return the crates to specific locations,  further impacting those who do not have access to vehicles. This could potentially affect customer loyalty and satisfaction.

 Space Constraints -  limited space in Singapore and FairPrice outlets may pose a challenge in accommodating for the collection points for the crates. As such, some stores may have to reduce in size to create space for collection, else the collection points would have to be located in obscure locations.

Compliance to Market Rules and Regulations -  Establishing a basket deposit scheme mandates compliance to regulatory requirements and with government policies. FairPrice would need to make an effort to ensure that its efforts align with regulations and obtain permits where needed.

Essay:
NTUC Fairprice should charge higher prices for plastic bags ($1) so as to encourage their customers to bring their own reusable bags and cut down on the amount of bags they buy from NTUC instead.

Currently, they are only charging 10-20 cents for 1 plastic bag which consumers conveniently use and purchase. Although the bigger population still uses plastic bags, this initiative by Fairprice has already saved 57 million plastic bags in 2022. 

With Singaporeans known for their thriftiness in using money, the sharp increase in price is sure to affect an even wider population and really urge them to use their own reusable bags. 

Moreover, with a higher charge on plastic bags, the increase in revenue would enable Fairprice to switch to more environmentally friendly bags, including biodegradable plastic bags or high quality paper bags (follow European countries).

This could also encourage separate recycling processes for biodegradable plastic bags and non-biodegradable ones, instead of incinerating both together and having the same fate. 

With a higher charge on plastic bags (especially if the charge is meant to hurt economically), those of the lower socio-economic strata may be unfairly hurt by the charge as compared to everyone else. Therefore, the sense of responsibility to be environmentally conscious by bringing one’s own bag may be more vested in poorer communities than wealthier communities. To calibrate the charge, it should be at a level where everyone from all social stratas can be hurt, but not to the point of irreversibility. At the same time, if everyone of all social stratas are reasonably environmentally conscious, perhaps the difference in sense of responsibility amongst people may not be an issue at all. 
-	Concession card for plastic bags (CEPAS gets 50% off).

In conclusion, the revenue from a plastic bag charge should work toward an environmentally conscious endeavour, rather than simply economic gain. To achieve a reasonable abandonment of conventional plastic bags in favour for biodegradable ones, NTUC should increase its plastic bag charge and use the revenue to produce biodegradable bags

Question:
1.Should we focus on economic growth and development or prioritize environmental injustice when addressing social inclusion? Explain your answer.
2.How do we reconcile the potential conflicts between economic progress and environmental injustice in pursuing social equity?
Essay:
Pushing for environmental justice and economic progress go hand-in-hand – in order for the economy to best serve its people, people must be able to work and live in conditions that are liveable. This means that the climate must be taken care of in order for workers to best fuel the economy as well. In fact, economic progress that truly reduces the GINI coefficient and brings more people into basic living conditions would enable them to put more focus on the environment and social issues. As such, ensuring that both environmental justice and economic progress are looked after is an important issue to improve the wellbeing of people.

Environmental injustice often disproportionately affects vulnerable populations. By placing emphasis on environmental justice, social workers can advocate for policies and practices that promote sustainable development, fair working conditions, and equitable distribution of resources, contributing to a more inclusive and just society. In pushing for environmental and economic sustainability, we need to advocate for those who have been silenced, and have been disproportionately affected by both climate and economic inequalities, such as migrant workers who are transported dangerously in lorries and are housed in crowded dormitories. Policies need to be focused on eradicating the oppression and exploitation of marginalised communities while uplifting them. People tend to favour environmental justice and social inclusion only after their basic needs are met. This is fair, because how can they (be expected to) engage in individualised green efforts when (1) they do not have the means to, and (2) they are not the ones who are driving the climate crisis.

At the same time, investments should go towards green technologies to ensure that measures are put in place to minimise and reduce carbon emissions and their effects. Alongside this, preventive measures like the carbon tax must be heightened and put in place to hold corporations responsible for their significant contributions to the climate crisis and environmental degradation.

Democracy is also key in ensuring healthy feedback loops and to implement policies that serve everyone. Let’s provide those who are affected with a voice to empower their needs. During policy planning, public consultation must be conducted with people who are most affected by either environmental injustice and economic injustice. In this manner, potential conflicts may be resolved and marginalised individuals will not be neglected, hence, allowing for social equity. 

The pursuit of social equity should involve inclusive policies that consider the well-being of both the population and the environment, aiming for the coexistence between economic progress and environmental sustainability.

Question:
1.Should we focus on economic growth and development or prioritize environmental injustice when addressing social inclusion? Explain your answer.
2.How do we reconcile the potential conflicts between economic progress and environmental injustice in pursuing social equity?
Essay:
We are focusing on addressing environmental injustice as we believe that it serves to benefit more people compared to economic development which we believe mainly benefits the ruling elites and those who are already well-to-do. Environmental injustice issues also tend to be related to basic human needs (e.g., access to drinking water, having sufficient food etc.). Such needs cannot be neglected and should be a prerequisite before economic development can take place. Environmental issues should also be addressed first as it might be more costly to solve it as time progresses due to global warming etc. Thus, addressing environmental injustice helps to narrow the gap between the rich and poor, allowing everyone to receive the same resources, thus enhancing social cohesion.

However, we should not neglect the fact that economic growth can lead to greater innovation regarding more sustainable practices (ie. using cleaner forms of energy, minimising pollution during production processes etc), which could improve the overall standard of living in Singapore.

To address any potential conflicts, our group believes that governmental policies are important. The government should have clear policies and regulations to ‘balance’ between economic growth and environmental issues. An example would be to provide tax rebates for companies and corporations that adopt environmentally friendly practices in order to incentivise them to promote sustainable growth. 

Additionally, there should also be policies such as subsidies to make basic necessities such as food (in the form of e.g. CDC vouchers to lower-income families) and water more affordable for the lower-income individuals. Such subsidies can be implemented based on the pre-existing CHAS card program, where individuals with lower tiered cards could receive greater discounts when they purchase necessities islandwide.

Q1: We believe that when addressing social inclusion, there is no one-size-fits-all ideal on what we should focus on. Differing perspectives and situations require for differing focuses between economic growth and development and environmental injustice.
In the perspective of advanced economies, there can be a greater focus on environmental injustices. When the basic needs of the society such as having enough food and healthcare services has been fulfilled, society will then be willing to pay for environmental protection, and a greater focus can be placed on environmental injustice. This is a global phenomenon whereby high GDP countries such as Denmark, which is the World’s Most Sustainable Country with the highest Environmental Performance Index of 77.9 in 2022, has one of the highest GDPs in the world.

In the case of developing and less developed countries where access to resources is limited, we should consider focusing more on economic growth. When struggling to make ends meet, one would never think about the environmental impacts that they may incur but would do their utmost to alleviate the situation to try to achieve financial stability. Similarly, investing in environmental injustice would mean high costs incurred just for adaptation to our current environment. This can be seen in research done by the IMF and others, which suggests public adaptation costs will reach around 0.25 percent of global gross domestic product per year in the coming decades.
Diverting resources in these countries for environmental improvements would instead result in greater detrimental impacts in economic and social aspects.
